analogy.p: Imagine a sealed room with thousands of tennis balls bouncing off the walls, floor and ceiling. The walls feel a steady push from all the hits. If the balls are thrown faster (hotter gas), they hit the walls more often and harder, so the push on the walls is larger. If you remove balls (less gas) or enlarge the room, hits become rarer and the push becomes weaker. Where it breaks down: tennis balls lose energy and stop bouncing, whereas gas molecules collide elastically and keep their energy, and real molecules are far smaller and numerous (about 10^25 per cubic metre) than the balls.
analogy.t: A room full of bouncing tennis balls

bullets: The molecules of a gas are in **constant random motion**.
The **temperature** of a gas is related to the **average kinetic energy** of its molecules.
Changing the temperature of a gas held at **constant volume** changes the **pressure** the gas exerts.
You must link **two** ideas in every explanation: how often molecules hit the walls and how hard they hit.
Check you can write the explanation as a four-step chain of cause and effect, because most 4-mark questions are marked step by step.
This point leads directly to **pressure and volume of a gas** (the next point), where temperature is constant instead.
core.p: This point is part of the **particle model of matter** (physics only content in AQA). You must be able to explain how the **motion of the molecules in a gas** is related to both its **temperature** and its **pressure**, and to explain **qualitatively** the relation between the **temperature of a gas and its pressure at constant volume**. 'Qualitatively' means you describe the pattern and explain it in words using the particle model, rather than calculating with a formula. Mark schemes reward a clear chain: temperature → particle speed/kinetic energy → collisions with the walls → force → pressure.

bullets: Gas molecules are **widely spaced**, so most of the volume of a gas is empty space.
They move **randomly** and **continuously**; their paths are straight lines between collisions.
The forces between them are **very weak** (negligible), so a gas expands to fill any container.
Different molecules in the same gas move at **different speeds**; the speeds keep changing as molecules collide and exchange energy.
Evidence for the motion: **Brownian motion**, where visible smoke particles in air jiggle randomly because they are hit unevenly by fast, invisible air molecules.
Collisions are **elastic on average**: the gas does not lose energy overall, so it does not slow down and stop.
The mass of the gas is the total mass of its molecules; the **volume** is that of the container, not of the molecules.
core.h: The particle model of a gas
core.p: In a gas the particles (atoms or molecules) are **far apart** compared with their size, move **randomly in all directions at high speed**, and have **negligible forces of attraction** between them except when they collide. Because there is so much empty space, gases have a **low density** and can be **compressed** easily. The particles travel in straight lines until they collide with another particle or with the walls of the container, and they change direction at each collision.

bullets: **Higher temperature = higher average kinetic energy = faster average speed.**
Temperature is about the **average**: some molecules are much faster and some much slower than the average in a sample at one temperature.
At the same temperature, **lighter molecules** move faster on average than heavier ones because they have the same average KE (e.g. hydrogen moves faster than oxygen).
If the temperature falls, the average kinetic energy falls; at the lowest possible temperature (**absolute zero**) the molecules would have the minimum possible energy.
The **internal energy** of a gas is the total of the kinetic and potential energies of its particles; for an ideal gas with negligible forces, nearly all of this is kinetic.
Heating a gas can increase the temperature, as the particles gain kinetic energy; this is different from a change of state, where energy goes into potential energy.
Link: the thermal energy supplied to a gas raises the particles' kinetic energy, which is the same idea as in specific heat capacity.
core.p: The temperature of a gas depends on how fast its molecules move **on average**. More precisely, the **temperature is related to the average kinetic energy** of the molecules. When a gas is heated, energy is transferred to the molecules and their average kinetic energy increases, so on average they move **faster**. When a gas is cooled, the opposite happens. Kinetic energy depends on mass and speed (KE = ½ m v²), so at the same temperature the average kinetic energy of molecules is the same whatever the gas.

bullets: The molecule hits the wall, its direction reverses (component at right angles to the wall), so its **momentum changes**; by Newton's laws the wall experiences a force.
The **net force** from many random collisions acts **at right angles to the surface**, because sideways components cancel out.
Gas pressure acts **equally in all directions** inside a container.
**Pressure = force ÷ area**, so a larger force on the same area, or the same force on a smaller area, gives higher pressure.
A gas pressure depends on: the **number of collisions per second**, and the **force of each collision**.
Both factors are changed when the temperature of the gas changes, as explained in the next section.
Atmospheric pressure at sea level is about **100 000 Pa (1.0 × 10^5 Pa)**, due to the weight of air above (and molecular collisions).
core.p: Gas pressure is caused by molecules **colliding with the walls** of the container (or any surface in the gas). Each collision exerts a tiny **force** on the wall because the molecule's **momentum changes** as it rebounds. A gas has an enormous number of molecules, so there are billions of collisions every second, and these produce a steady **net force at right angles to the wall**. Pressure is the force per unit area: **p = F ÷ A**, measured in **pascals (Pa)**, where 1 Pa = 1 N/m².

bullets: Step 1: **temperature increases**, so the **average kinetic energy** of the molecules increases (they move faster on average).
Step 2: the molecules travel the container faster, so they **hit the walls more frequently** (more collisions per second).
Step 3: each collision has a **larger change of momentum**, so the molecules exert a **greater force** on the wall in each collision.
Step 4: the total force per unit area increases, so the **pressure increases**.
The same chain in reverse explains why **cooling** a gas in a fixed volume **reduces** the pressure.
The volume is **constant** and the **number of molecules** is constant; if either changes, the explanation changes.
For the exam, always name **both** frequency and force of collisions; saying only 'more collisions' usually gains half marks.
Remember to say 'on average': not every molecule moves faster, only the average kinetic energy increases.
core.h: Why heating a gas at constant volume raises its pressure
core.p: Consider a **sealed rigid container** so the volume and the number of molecules cannot change. If the gas is heated, its temperature rises. The explanation is a chain of four linked points, and all four are needed for full marks: the molecules gain kinetic energy and move faster; they hit the walls more often; each collision is harder (a larger change in momentum, so a larger force); therefore the total force on the walls, and so the pressure, increases.

bullets: **0 K = −273 °C** (absolute zero); **273 K = 0 °C** (ice melts); **373 K = 100 °C** (water boils).
A temperature **difference** is the same in K and °C (a rise of 10 °C is a rise of 10 K).
Kelvin temperatures can **never be negative**, as nothing can be colder than absolute zero.
At absolute zero the pressure of a gas at constant volume would extrapolate to **zero**, because the molecules would (in the model) have no kinetic energy to hit the walls.
Real gases turn into liquids before reaching absolute zero, so the zero-pressure point is found by **extrapolating** a graph.
Doubling the **Kelvin** temperature doubles the average kinetic energy; doubling the Celsius temperature does not.
core.h: The Kelvin scale and absolute zero
core.p: Because molecular speeds cannot be negative, there is a lowest possible temperature. **Absolute zero** is **0 K (−273 °C)**, the temperature at which the molecules have the **minimum possible kinetic energy**. The **Kelvin scale** starts at absolute zero, and a temperature change of 1 K is the same size as a change of 1 °C. To convert, **K = °C + 273** and **°C = K − 273**. The Kelvin scale is the natural scale for gases because the pressure of a gas at constant volume is proportional to its Kelvin temperature.

bullets: Graph of pressure (y) against temperature in °C: **straight line, positive gradient, not through the origin**.
The extrapolated line cuts the temperature axis at **−273 °C**, which is **absolute zero**.
Graph of pressure against temperature in K: **straight line through the origin**, so **pressure ∝ Kelvin temperature** (constant volume).
Extension (not required for GCSE calculation): for a fixed mass at constant volume, **p ÷ T = constant**, so p₁ ÷ T₁ = p₂ ÷ T₂, with T in kelvin.
A straight line shows a constant ratio; a curve would mean the relationship is not simply proportional.
In practice the investigation uses a sealed flask connected to a pressure gauge, heated in a water bath, with temperature recorded by a thermometer.
Exam tip: when describing the graph, give the **shape**, the **direction** and what the intercept means.
core.h: The pressure-temperature relationship at constant volume
core.p: Experiments show that for a fixed mass of gas at constant volume, pressure increases steadily as temperature increases. If you plot **pressure against temperature in °C**, you get a straight line that does not pass through the origin; if you extend (**extrapolate**) the line back, it meets the temperature axis at **−273 °C**, where the pressure would be zero. If you plot pressure against temperature in **kelvin**, the line goes through the origin, showing the pressure is **directly proportional** to the Kelvin temperature. Qualitatively you only need to say that pressure increases as temperature increases.

bullets: A single molecule's speed is **random** and unpredictable; the average over very many molecules is predictable.
A hot gas still contains some slow molecules, and a cold gas some fast ones, but the **average** differs.
The very large number (about 10^25 molecules per cubic metre of air) of collisions smooths out into a **constant pressure**.
If you reduce the amount of gas (fewer molecules) at the same temperature and volume, the **pressure decreases** because there are fewer collisions per second.
The speed distribution **spreads** and shifts to higher speeds as temperature rises.
This is why exam answers say 'average kinetic energy' and 'on average' for full marks.
Higher tier extension: at the same temperature, average KE is the same for all gases, so the molecules of a **lighter** gas have a higher average **speed** since KE = ½ m v².
core.p: Statements about gases are about **large numbers** of molecules. Individual molecules move at a wide range of speeds, and their speeds change as they collide and exchange energy. When we say 'the molecules move faster when it is hotter' we mean **on average**: the whole range of speeds shifts upward. Because there are so many molecules, the average behaviour is extremely stable, which is why the pressure of a gas looks like a steady push rather than a series of individual hits.

bullets: **Car tyres:** after a long journey the tyre gets warmer, the air molecules move faster and hit the inside walls harder and more often, so the pressure increases; tyre pressure is checked when the tyres are **cold**.
**Aerosol cans or sealed containers:** heating them raises the gas pressure inside and they may **explode**, which is why warnings say keep away from heat.
**Pressure cooker:** the steam and air are sealed, so the pressure rises as the temperature rises, allowing the water to boil above 100 °C and cook faster.
**Sealed flask in a water bath:** a pressure gauge shows the pressure rising as the water is heated.
**A dented ping pong ball placed in hot water** pops out because the air inside gains kinetic energy and its pressure increases.
**Cooling:** a sealed plastic bottle left in a freezer shrinks because the pressure inside falls; the higher pressure outside pushes it inwards.
**Hot-air balloon** (open at the bottom): the pressure stays about atmospheric; instead the gas expands and becomes less dense. Do not confuse this with a sealed container.
core.p: Gas pressure and temperature appear in many practical situations, and examiners often use them as unfamiliar contexts. In each case the volume is fixed (or nearly fixed) and the gas is heated or cooled, so you apply exactly the same four-step explanation. The trick is to identify what is constant (volume, amount of gas) and what changes (temperature).

bullets: **Internal energy** (previous point): temperature rises mean the kinetic energy part of the internal energy rises.
**Specific latent heat** (previous point): a change of state is different because energy goes into potential energy, not into the temperature rise.
**Pressure and volume** (next point): at constant temperature, a smaller volume means more frequent collisions, so a higher pressure (p V = constant).
**Forces:** the force from the gas acts at right angles to the surface; a gas can do work when it expands, for example pushing a piston.
**Momentum and Newton's third law:** the wall pushes on the molecule and the molecule pushes on the wall with equal and opposite forces.
**Atmospheric pressure** and altitude: higher up, there are fewer air molecules above, so the pressure decreases.
**Planning an investigation:** independent variable: temperature; dependent: pressure; control: volume of gas, mass of gas (sealed).
**Command words:** 'explain' needs the chain of reasoning; 'describe' the pattern; 'suggest' links the idea to a new context.
core.h: Links to other topics and exam strategy
core.p: This topic ties together **energy**, **forces** and **the particle model**. The kinetic energy of molecules links to energy stores and internal energy, the force on the walls links to Newton's laws and momentum, and pressure links to the pressure equations used in fluids. It also connects directly to the next point, **pressure and volume of a gas**, where the temperature is held constant and you explain why reducing the volume increases the pressure.

bullets: Describe the shape first: straight line, positive gradient (pressure rises as temperature rises).
In °C: the line has a positive intercept on the pressure axis, so it is **not** directly proportional.
Extrapolating back to p = 0 gives about **−273 °C** (0 K).
In K: a straight line through the origin means **p ∝ T**, so doubling T doubles p.
Extrapolation is used because real gases condense before reaching absolute zero, so the low-temperature part cannot be measured.
Constant gradient means p ÷ T is constant, which gives p₁ ÷ T₁ = p₂ ÷ T₂ (extension).
Always state the conditions: fixed mass of gas and fixed volume.
core.h: Describing and using the pressure-temperature graph
core.p: A graph of pressure against temperature for a fixed mass of gas at constant volume is a **straight line with a positive gradient**. When the temperature is plotted in **degrees Celsius** the line does **not** pass through the origin, so the pressure is not directly proportional to the Celsius temperature. If the line is **extrapolated** (extended beyond the measured data) it meets the pressure = 0 axis at **−273 °C**, which defines absolute zero. When temperature is plotted in **kelvin** the same line passes through the **origin**, so pressure is **directly proportional** to the kelvin temperature. The graph also shows the particle-model idea that pressure depends on the average kinetic energy of the molecules.

bullets: Fixed volume: the molecules cannot spread out, so the only change is their speed.
Fixed number of molecules: no gas is added or lost, so the number density is unchanged.
The molecules do not get **bigger** or **hotter** individually: the **average** kinetic energy rises.
Pressure is not caused by molecules hitting **each other**, but by hitting the **walls**.
Do not say the molecules 'expand' when heated: the container (volume) is fixed in this point.
Pressure acts equally in all directions, so it does not matter which wall you consider.
If asked about a flexible container such as a balloon, say the volume can change, so this simple explanation does not apply.
core.h: Reasoning traps: what must stay the same
core.p: Most lost marks on this topic come from not saying **what is being kept constant**, or from mixing up the effect of temperature with the effect of changing volume. In this point the **volume** and the **number of molecules** are fixed, so the only thing changing is the speed of the molecules. If the container could expand, the molecules would travel further between collisions, which is the separate idea of **pressure and volume** covered in the next point. Keep your explanation focused: temperature up, speed up, collision frequency up, force per collision up, pressure up.

exam: **Define/state (1 mark):** pressure = force per unit area; temperature related to the average kinetic energy of the molecules.

**Explain a pressure rise on heating (4 marks):** (1) molecules gain kinetic energy / move faster, (2) hit the walls more often, (3) with a greater force (each collision), (4) so pressure increases because volume is constant.
**2-mark answers:** 'molecules move faster' + 'more frequent / harder collisions with the walls'; always say with the walls.
**Graph question (2-3 marks):** describe the shape (straight line, positive), the intercept (−273 °C, absolute zero) and say pressure is zero when extrapolated.
**Convert temperatures (1-2 marks):** show K = °C + 273; give an answer in K or °C as asked.
**Constant volume statement:** always state that the volume and mass of gas are constant in your explanation.
**Reverse questions:** when the gas is cooled, the molecules slow, hit the walls less often and less hard, so pressure falls.
**6-mark questions:** link temperature, kinetic energy, collisions (frequency and force), pressure, and give an example such as a car tyre or aerosol can.
**Command words:** 'explain' needs reasons (because); 'describe' just the pattern; 'suggest' apply to a new context.
**Say 'average':** use average kinetic energy for full marks; avoid saying 'all molecules'.
**Units:** pressure in Pa (N/m²), force in N, area in m²; convert cm² to m² (1 m² = 10 000 cm²).

mistakes.r: The molecules do not change size; they gain kinetic energy and move faster.
mistakes.w: The molecules get bigger or expand when heated.

mistakes.r: Pressure is caused by collisions with the walls of the container, not between molecules.
mistakes.w: Pressure increases because the molecules collide with each other more.

mistakes.r: Also say the collisions are harder (greater force each) because the molecules move faster; mention both frequency and force.
mistakes.w: The molecules hit the wall more often, so pressure increases (stopping there).

mistakes.r: The average kinetic energy increases; the range of speeds shifts higher but individual molecules vary.
mistakes.w: All the molecules move faster when heated.

mistakes.r: Temperature is related to the average kinetic energy of the molecules; heat is energy transferred.
mistakes.w: Temperature is the same as heat or energy.

mistakes.r: Pressure is proportional to the temperature in kelvin, not °C; convert with K = °C + 273.
Gas pressure acts equally in all directions, at right angles to any surface, because of molecular collisions.
mistakes.w: Gas pressure acts downwards because of gravity.

mistakes.r: Molecules keep moving until absolute zero (0 K, −273 °C), the lowest possible temperature.
mistakes.w: Cooling a gas makes the molecules stop moving at 0 °C.

summary: Explain how the random motion of gas molecules produces pressure through collisions with the walls, how temperature relates to the average kinetic energy, and explain qualitatively why increasing the temperature of a gas at constant volume increases its pressure. This matters because it is the basis for the pressure and volume of a gas and many practical safety situations.

terms.d: The force exerted per unit area on a surface by gas molecules colliding with it; it acts at right angles to the surface.
The unit of pressure; 1 Pa = 1 N/m².
The mean kinetic energy of the molecules in a sample; the temperature of a gas is related to it.
Movement in all directions with no pattern; gas molecules move randomly and continuously.
The temperature scale in which 0 K is absolute zero; a change of 1 K equals a change of 1 °C.
The lowest possible temperature, 0 K or −273 °C, where particles have the minimum possible kinetic energy.
The container size is fixed, so the volume of the gas does not change when its temperature changes.
The total kinetic energy and potential energy of all the particles in a system.
An interaction in which particles exchange momentum and energy; collisions with a wall produce a force.
When a molecule rebounds from a wall its momentum reverses, so the wall experiences a force.
Two quantities whose ratio is constant; the graph is a straight line through the origin.
Extend a line on a graph beyond the measured data to estimate where it would go.
The random jiggling of visible particles in a fluid caused by collisions with fast moving, invisible molecules.
The model that explains the behaviour of gases in terms of the random motion of their particles.

worked.ans: Full-mark answer: The molecules gain kinetic energy and move faster on average. They collide with the walls more frequently and with greater force each time. Since the volume is fixed, the total force on each unit area of the wall increases, so the pressure increases.
worked.q: A sealed, rigid metal container of air is heated. Explain, in terms of the motion of the molecules, why the pressure of the air increases. (4 marks)
steps: Heating raises the temperature, so the average kinetic energy of the molecules increases (they move faster).
The molecules hit the walls more often.
Each collision exerts a bigger force on the wall (larger change in momentum).
The container volume is constant, so total force per unit area on the walls increases.
